120: I protect priceless treasures by standing here. Very still. Thinking, mostly, about lunch.
121: My job is to not touch the art, and to stop anyone else touching it. Mostly I stop myself.
122: I've stood before this painting for nine years. I still don't know what it is about.
123: I guard a room full of ancient gold. My chair squeaks. That is the only excitement.
124: People whisper in my museum out of respect. I whisper because I am half asleep.
125: I watch the art all day. Sometimes the art seems to watch me back. We have an understanding.
126: My great skill is standing perfectly still. I have been mistaken for a statue four times.
127: The most valuable thing here is behind glass. The second most valuable is my chair.
128: I protect history itself. Right now history is quiet, and I am counting the ceiling tiles.
129: I let nothing past this door. Not a person, not a fly. Especially not a fly. Flies keep me busy.
130: I stand guard from morning to night. The paintings never leave. Neither, it seems, do I.
131: Someone asked what I do all day. I stand here and watch, I said. They called it boring. Accurate.
132: I've memorized every crack in this old floor. It's a hobby now. It's the only hobby.
133: My uniform says security. My feet say sit down. We argue about this all day.
134: I guard treasures worth more than my whole town. And I am thinking about a sandwich.
135: There is an alarm for emergencies. In fifteen years it has rung twice. Both times, my elbow.
136: The rule is simple: don't let anyone take the art. So far, wonderfully, nobody has tried.
137: I watch a golden vase all day. It does nothing. I do nothing. We are a good team.
138: Visitors think this job is glamorous. Then they see me stretching my back very slowly.
139: I could name every painting here with my eyes closed. Some days I do, to pass the time.
140: I point at old things and explain why they matter. People nod. I love the nodding.
141: My job is to make a very old pot sound thrilling. Some days I even believe it myself.
142: I give the tour twelve times a day. By noon I could give it asleep. Sometimes I do.
143: I stop at each object and say something meaningful. The objects have heard it all before.
144: I lead groups through the museum. My whole skill is walking slowly and pointing well.
145: I explained a chair for ten minutes today. A very old, very important chair. Nobody sat.
146: I say 'and if you look here' about forty times a day. My finger is the hardest worker.
147: People come to learn. I come to point at things. Together we make a lovely afternoon.
148: My tour has a big finish. It is a small vase. I've learned to build the suspense anyway.
149: I know a hundred stories about these objects. The objects have never once thanked me.
150: On today's tour a small boy asked if the statue was alive. I said no. He wasn't convinced. Fair.
151: I walk backwards while I talk so I can face the group. I have not fallen yet. Yet.
152: I describe every brushstroke of a painting. It takes twenty minutes. The painting waits.
153: My greatest tool is my pointing hand. My second is knowing when to stop pointing.
154: I lead people from room to room, explaining. It's just slow, very well-informed walking.
155: I've given this tour so often the objects feel like coworkers. Quiet coworkers. Old ones.
156: I make history come alive. Mostly by talking about it until someone's stomach growls.
157: The tour ends exactly where it began. A tidy loop. My feet have filed a complaint about the loop.
158: I point at a thousand-year-old jar and everyone gasps. I did the gasp first, years ago.
159: My job is enthusiasm about the past. It's easier before lunch. The past waits patiently.
